claims.text: Premelting and melting in HEA nanoparticles are primarily governed by surface segregation of lower-melting elements.
Heating causes lower-melting elements to diffuse to the nanoparticle surface.
Differential elemental segregation produces a chemically heterogeneous surface with lower local bonding strength or cohesive energy than the particle interior.
The weakened segregated surface forms an early disordered premelt layer.
The segregated premelt layer triggers melting of the overall nanoparticle and lowers its melting temperature relative to a uniformly mixed or bulk counterpart.
The high surface energy of HEA nanoparticles drives differential diffusion during heating.
Lower-melting or more mobile alloy species preferentially migrate to the surface.
Mild post-annealing promotes surface mobility and segregation in these HEA nanoparticles.
A thin conformal inert coating such as alumina suppresses elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surface.
Segregated or segregation-promoted nanoparticles will exhibit premelting or melting at a lower temperature than uniformly mixed HEA nanoparticles or bulk HEAs.
Surface segregation should dominate premelting behavior in HEA nanoparticles smaller than approximately 100 nm.
The influence of surface segregation on melting should diminish in larger particles and bulk materials because their surface contribution is smaller.
Support interactions or passivation layers can modify the degree of surface segregation.
Multicomponent nanoparticles are relevant to catalysis, sensing, and energy-storage applications.
Loading nanoparticles on supports can increase their specific surface area and surface energy relative to bulk materials or unsupported nanoparticles.
Equimolar PtPdNiFeCu nanoparticles can be synthesized with an initially uniform elemental distribution and high dispersion on inert supports.
For the contemplated HEA nanoparticles, a 500–1000 °C heating range extends to well above the expected nanoparticle melting temperature.
In situ TEM can identify the temperature at which a disordered surface layer appears.
DSC can resolve a downward shift in melting-onset temperature between the compared nanoparticle sets.
